issues.legal_issue: Succession to a non-hereditary religious office is governed by the institution’s proved custom, including both the eligibility of candidates and the authority and manner of appointment.
material_facts: The institution’s custom was that the Bhek and the worshippers appointed the successor; a disciple of the deceased Mahant had priority, but if there was no disciple, a spiritually related person such as a Bhatija chela could be appointed.
The Court found that the deceased Mahant had left no disciple and that the claimant was his spiritual collateral and thus eligible under the custom.
The Bhek and worshippers assembled and appointed the claimant, with the meeting attended by numerous local Bairagi Mahants and worshippers.

The evidence did not establish that formal invitations were customary, and the Court found no sufficient reason to reject the appointment because the presiding Mahant belonged to an allied Bairagi order.
issues.conclusion: The claimant was eligible and was validly appointed Mahant under the proved custom of the institution.
issues.legal_principle: Succession to Mahantship is regulated by the proved custom or usage of the particular institution, except where the founder has prescribed a rule. A disciple does not succeed automatically; the authority to appoint and the persons eligible for appointment depend on the institution’s custom. The Court relied on Genda Puri v. Chhatar Puri, 13 Ind App 100 (PC), for the requirement that entitlement be established according to custom, and referred to Jiwan Das v. Hira Das, AIR 1937 Lah 311, concerning appointment by the Bhek and worshippers.

rule.if: religious_office_succession_dispute and incumbent_left_no_disciple and claimant_is_spiritual_kindred and customary_appointing_body_selected_claimant

predicates.religious_office_succession_dispute: The proceeding concerns a dispute over succession to an office in a religious institution.
predicates.incumbent_left_no_disciple: The deceased office-holder left no disciple eligible to take priority under the institution’s custom.
predicates.claimant_is_spiritual_kindred: The claimant had the spiritual relationship required by the institution’s custom for appointment when no disciple was available.
predicates.customary_appointing_body_selected_claim: The body authorized by the institution’s custom selected the claimant for the office.

issues.definition: When a religious-office succession dispute concerns an incumbent who left no disciple, a spiritually related claimant selected by the customary appointing body is entitled to the office.

issues.legal_issue: A copy of an old document does not, merely because it is more than thirty years old, attract the presumption of due execution of the original when the copy is not properly admissible as secondary evidence.
material_facts: The defendants relied on a translation of an alleged copy of a will said to have been executed in 1911 to show that the deceased Mahant had taken the defendant as a disciple.
The original will and a certified copy were not produced, the document had not been proved by a witness, and no foundation had been laid for its admission as secondary evidence.
The Court found that the translation of the alleged copy could not be treated as secondary evidence within the Evidence Act.
issues.conclusion: The alleged 1911 will was not proved, and its translation was excluded from consideration.
issues.legal_principle: Section 90 of the Indian Evidence Act requires production of the particular document for which the presumption is sought; production of an admissible copy may at most support a presumption concerning the copy’s authenticating signatures, not due execution of the original. A copy must also qualify as secondary evidence under sections 63 and 65. The Court relied on Basant Singh v. Brij Raj Saran Singh, AIR 1935 PC 132.

rule.if: civil_evidentiary_dispute and party_relies_on_old_document and only_unproved_copy_produced and copy_not_admissible_as_secondary_evidence

predicates.civil_evidentiary_dispute: The proceeding requires the court to decide whether a document proves a disputed fact.
predicates.party_relies_on_old_document: A party relies on a document said to be more than thirty years old.
predicates.only_unproved_copy_produced: The party produces only a copy that has not otherwise been proved.
predicates.copy_not_admissible_as_secondary_evidenc: The requirements for admitting the copy as secondary evidence have not been established.

issues.definition: In a civil evidentiary dispute, an old document’s age does not prove execution of the original when the party produces only an unproved copy that is not admissible as secondary evidence.

issues.legal_issue: A prior judgment may be received as evidence of a transaction in which a person asserted a relevant right, even though the judgment is not an admission by that person under the Evidence Act.
material_facts: A prior judgment recorded a spiritual pedigree connecting the deceased Mahant and the claimant through a common spiritual ancestor.
The deceased Mahant had been a plaintiff in that earlier proceeding and had asserted a right as a spiritual collateral of the person whose property alienation was challenged.
The evidence did not establish who had propounded the pedigree recorded in the earlier judgment, so it could not be treated as an admission by the deceased Mahant.
The Court considered the judgment together with the oral evidence supporting the claimant’s spiritual relationship.
issues.conclusion: The prior judgment was admissible under section 13 as evidence of a transaction asserting the relevant right, though it was not conclusive and had to be weighed with the other evidence.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13 of the Indian Evidence Act permits evidence of a transaction in which a right was asserted or recognized; the earlier judgment could be used on that basis. The pedigree was not an admission under section 21 because it was not shown to have been propounded by the person against whom it was relied upon.

predicates.civil_proceeding_involves_disputed_right: The proceeding concerns whether a person holds a disputed right.
predicates.prior_judgment_records_transaction_asser: An earlier judgment records a transaction in which a person asserted or obtained recognition of a right relevant to the present dispute.
predicates.judgment_is_not_shown_to_be_party_admiss: The evidence does not show that the relevant statement in the earlier judgment was an admission made or adopted by the party against whom it is now used.

issues.definition: A prior judgment recording a transaction asserting a relevant right is admissible evidence of that assertion even when it is not established as an admission by the opposing party.

issues.legal_issue: A person claiming succession under a custom that gives priority to a disciple cannot establish eligibility merely by showing appointment when an eligible disciple of the deceased office-holder existed.
material_facts: The proved custom gave a disciple of the deceased Mahant priority for appointment, while permitting appointment of spiritual kindred if no disciple remained.
The defendants claimed that one of them was a disciple of the deceased Mahant and relied on alleged wills and testimony to establish that relationship.
The Court considered land records, a ration card, commercial records, the defendant’s evidence, and the absence of evidence of initiation rites.
The Court found that the defendant’s status as a disciple had not been proved and that the deceased Mahant had left no disciple.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the defendant had not been proved to be a disciple of the deceased Mahant; it was therefore unnecessary to decide whether he had been appointed by the Bhek and worshippers.
issues.legal_principle: The claimant to Mahantship must establish entitlement under the institution’s custom; where that custom gives a disciple priority, proof that the alleged disciple was in fact a disciple is material. Relevant official records may be considered under section 35 of the Indian Evidence Act. The Court also rejected reliance on the alleged old will under section 90 and applied Basant Singh v. Brij Raj Saran Singh, AIR 1935 PC 132, to the copy of that will.

predicates.religious_office_succession_dispute: The proceeding concerns a dispute over succession to an office in a religious institution.
predicates.custom_gives_disciple_priority: The institution’s proved custom gives a disciple of the deceased office-holder priority for appointment.
predicates.alleged_disciple_status_is_unproved: The evidence does not establish that the person claiming priority was a disciple of the deceased office-holder.

issues.definition: In a religious-office succession dispute, a person cannot establish priority under a custom favoring disciples when the evidence does not prove that the person was a disciple.

issues.legal_issue: A lease of endowed property is not binding on the institution unless those relying on it establish that it was supported by necessity or was a prudent transaction in the ordinary course of management.
material_facts: The deceased Mahant granted a ten-year lease of endowed land shortly before his death.
The lease recited payment of a premium that the trial court found had not been paid, and the rent was found to be grossly inadequate compared with the property’s ordinary profits.
The lessees offered no evidence about the property’s potential profits or the adequacy of the rent and did not testify.
The finding that the lease was unsupported by legal necessity was not challenged in the High Court.
issues.conclusion: The lessees failed to prove that the lease was a prudent act of management, and the lease was not binding on the institution.
issues.legal_principle: A lease that is not permanent may be supportable as a transaction in the ordinary course of management, but those relying on it bear the burden of showing that it was a prudent act within the manager’s competence. The Court applied the ordinary-course-of-management principle and the burden of proof as to the lease’s prudence.

predicates.challenge_to_lease_of_endowed_property: The proceeding challenges a lease of property held for a religious institution or endowment.
predicates.lease_is_not_permanent: The challenged lease is for a limited term rather than a permanent alienation.
predicates.party_relying_on_lease_bears_management_: The party seeking to uphold the lease must show that it was a prudent transaction within the manager’s authority.
predicates.consideration_or_rent_is_unsubstantiated: The stated consideration is not proved or the rent is shown to be inadequate, and the party relying on the lease does not substantiate its fairness.

issues.definition: A limited-term lease of endowed property is not binding when it is challenged and those relying on it fail to substantiate the consideration or rent needed to show prudent management.
